listening.title: Campus Music Room Reservation
listening.script:
Receptionist (Mr. Davies): Good morning, Riverside Campus Music Centre, you're speaking with Tom Davies. How can I help you?
Maya: Good morning, Mr. Davies. My name is Maya Patel. I'm a first-year student. I want to book a music room for piano practice.
Mr. Davies: Of course, Maya. Which day would you like?
Maya: This Thursday, please. In the afternoon.
Mr. Davies: Let me check. We have Room A and Room B free on Thursday. Room A has an upright piano, Room B has a grand piano.
Maya: I prefer the grand piano, so Room B, please.
Mr. Davies: Room B is free from 2 p.m. to 6 p.m. What time do you want?
Maya: From 3 p.m. to 5 p.m. would be great.
Mr. Davies: Actually, sorry, I made a mistake. Room B is booked at 3 p.m. for a lesson. It's free from 4 p.m. to 6 p.m. Is 4 to 6 okay?
Maya: Yes, 4 to 6 is fine.
Mr. Davies: Great. How long will you need it regularly? Just this week?
Maya: Just this Thursday for now. Maybe every week later.
Mr. Davies: Okay. There is a small fee of $5 per hour, so $10 for two hours. You can pay at the desk.
Maya: That's fine. Do I need to bring anything?
Mr. Davies: Please bring your student ID card to show at reception. Also, please don't bring food or drinks into the room.
Maya: I understand. No food or drinks. Can I bring my friend to listen?
Mr. Davies: Yes, one guest is allowed, but they must be quiet.
Mr. Davies: So to confirm, Maya Patel, Room B this Thursday from 4 to 6 p.m., $10, bring ID.
Mr. Davies: Your booking number is M-442. Please keep it for Thursday.
Maya: M-442, got it. Can I book online next time?
Mr. Davies: Yes, after today you can book on the campus website.
Maya: Perfect. Thank you very much.
Mr. Davies: You're welcome. See you Thursday.

reading.title: Student Bicycle Safety Workshop
reading.passage:
Last month, Greenfield College held a free bicycle safety workshop for students. The college is in a busy town where many students ride bicycles to classes. Many students live close to the college, and cycling saves them money and time every day. In the last year, there were several small accidents near the campus gates. Student Services decided to organise a workshop to help students stay safe on the road.

The workshop took place on Saturday morning in the sports hall. About forty students attended. It was led by two guests: Officer Karen White from the town police and Sam Lee, a mechanic from the local bike shop. Officer White talked about road rules, such as stopping at red lights and using hand signals to turn. Sam Lee showed how to check a bicycle before riding. He explained the importance of testing brakes, checking tyre pressure, and using front and back lights at night. He also showed how a helmet should fit tightly and sit low on the forehead. The workshop lasted three hours and included time for questions. Each student also received a small booklet with safety tips to take home.

After the talks, students moved outside for practical training. The college had set up a short course in the car park with cones to mark turns and stops. Each student rode around the course while the leaders watched and gave advice. One student, Lisa, had thought her helmet fitted correctly before the workshop, but she found that it was too loose and moved when she shook her head. Sam helped her adjust the straps so it stayed firm. Many other students also learned that their lights were not bright enough.

The writer of this report believes the workshop was valuable mainly because it gave students more confidence, not only more information. For example, Lisa's loose helmet is just one case that shows a common problem, but the main point is that practical help makes students feel ready to cycle safely. Before the workshop, several students said they felt nervous in traffic. After practising, they said they felt calmer and more prepared.

Because the event was popular, Student Services will offer free monthly bicycle checks and free lights for students who need them. The next workshop will be in November. Teachers have also asked for a similar session for staff who cycle to work. The college hopes fewer accidents will happen and more students will enjoy cycling safely.

exercises.title: Student Bicycle Safety Workshop
exercises.passage:
Last month, Greenfield College held a free bicycle safety workshop for students. The college is in a busy town where many students ride bicycles to classes. Many students live close to the college, and cycling saves them money and time every day. In the last year, there were several small accidents near the campus gates. Student Services decided to organise a workshop to help students stay safe on the road.

The workshop took place on Saturday morning in the sports hall. About forty students attended. It was led by two guests: Officer Karen White from the town police and Sam Lee, a mechanic from the local bike shop. Officer White talked about road rules, such as stopping at red lights and using hand signals to turn. Sam Lee showed how to check a bicycle before riding. He explained the importance of testing brakes, checking tyre pressure, and using front and back lights at night. He also showed how a helmet should fit tightly and sit low on the forehead. The workshop lasted three hours and included time for questions. Each student also received a small booklet with safety tips to take home.

After the talks, students moved outside for practical training. The college had set up a short course in the car park with cones to mark turns and stops. Each student rode around the course while the leaders watched and gave advice. One student, Lisa, had thought her helmet fitted correctly before the workshop, but she found that it was too loose and moved when she shook her head. Sam helped her adjust the straps so it stayed firm. Many other students also learned that their lights were not bright enough.

The writer of this report believes the workshop was valuable mainly because it gave students more confidence, not only more information. For example, Lisa's loose helmet is just one case that shows a common problem, but the main point is that practical help makes students feel ready to cycle safely. Before the workshop, several students said they felt nervous in traffic. After practising, they said they felt calmer and more prepared.

Because the event was popular, Student Services will offer free monthly bicycle checks and free lights for students who need them. The next workshop will be in November. Teachers have also asked for a similar session for staff who cycle to work. The college hopes fewer accidents will happen and more students will enjoy cycling safely.
exercises.prompt: Why did Student Services organise the workshop?
options: To reduce accidents near campus gates
To sell bicycles to new students
To build a new sports hall
To train police officers in town
exercises.explanation: The text links recent accidents near the gates to the decision to help students stay safe. Selling bicycles was the bike shop's job, not the college's purpose.

The table below shows the number of students who attended three film-club screenings at Greenfield College from March to May 2024, and the percentage who said they enjoyed the film. Short Comedy Films | 70 | 65 | 55 | 85%
Classic Science Fiction | 30 | 40 | 48 | 62%

All screenings were on Friday evenings in Room B.

writingPrompts.focus: describing locations and changes clearly with simple comparisons
writingPrompts.prompt:
The maps below show the ground floor of Riverside City Museum in 2020 and in 2025. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. You should spend about 20 minutes on this task and write at least 150 words.

In 2020: The entrance was on the south side. Inside the entrance was a ticket desk. The Film Room was on the west side. The History Gallery was on the north-west corner. A small cafe was on the north-east corner. The gift shop was on the east side.

In 2025: The entrance is still on the south side. The ticket desk has moved to the east side, next to the gift shop. The Film Room is now larger and has moved to the north-west corner, where the History Gallery was. The History Gallery is now smaller and on the west side. There is a new Bicycle Display Area in the centre of the museum. The cafe is still in the north-east corner but is now larger.

writingPrompts.task: Task 1 · Introduction to Bicycle Maintenance Process
writingPrompts.focus: accurate simple explanations of a process in clear steps
writingPrompts.prompt:
The diagram below shows six steps to check a bicycle before riding. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features. You should spend about 20 minutes on this task and write at least 150 words.

Step 1: Check tyre pressure. If the tyres are soft, use a pump to add air.
Step 2: Check the brakes. Squeeze both brake levers and look at the brake pads.
Step 3: Check the chain. Clean the chain and add a little oil if it is dry.
Step 4: Check the lights and bell. Turn on the front and back lights and ring the bell to test them.
Step 5: Check the seat height. Sit on the seat and adjust it if your feet cannot touch the ground easily.
Step 6: Do a slow test ride in a safe area to make sure everything works.

writingPrompts.focus: clear main ideas with reasons and familiar examples
writingPrompts.prompt: Some people think schools should teach practical skills such as bicycle maintenance, cooking and basic repairs. Others think schools should only teach academic subjects like mathematics and science. Discuss both views and give your own opinion. Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience. You should spend about 40 minutes on this task and write at least 250 words.

writingPrompts.task: Task 2 · Community Film and Museum Activities
writingPrompts.focus: giving a clear position with direct evidence and simple explanations
writingPrompts.prompt: Many towns offer free activities such as student film-club screenings and local museum visits. Some people say these activities are very useful for students and local communities. Do you agree or disagree? Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience. You should spend about 40 minutes on this task and write at least 250 words.

speakingPrompts.focus: giving simple personal information and preferences
speakingPrompts.prompt:
Answer the following questions about films and free time. Speak for 30-60 seconds for each answer.
1. How often do you watch films?
2. Do you prefer watching films at home or at the cinema? Why?
3. Did you join any clubs when you were at school?
4. What do you usually do with friends in the evening?

speakingPrompts.focus: describing familiar places with simple explanations
speakingPrompts.prompt:
Answer the following questions about museums and your town. Speak for 30-60 seconds for each answer.
1. Is there a museum near where you live?
2. When was the last time you visited a museum?
3. Do you like looking at maps when you visit a new place? Why or why not?
4. How do you usually travel around your town - by bicycle, bus, or on foot?

speakingPrompts.task: Part 2 · Cue card · A Film Screening You Attended
speakingPrompts.focus: organising a short talk with clear sequence and details
speakingPrompts.prompt:
Describe a film screening or movie you watched together with other students or friends. You will have one minute to prepare and should speak for one to two minutes.

You should say:
• what the film was and where you watched it
• who you went with
• what happened during the screening
• and explain why you enjoyed it or not

You can finish with one short follow-up idea: Would you like to go to a similar screening again?

speakingPrompts.focus: giving reasons and evaluation about learning methods
speakingPrompts.prompt:
Discuss the following questions about practical skills such as bicycle maintenance. Give reasons and examples for your opinions.
1. Why is it useful for young people to learn practical skills?
2. Should schools or parents teach skills like bicycle repair? Why?
3. Is it better to learn a practical skill from a teacher, from a video, or by trying yourself? Why?

speakingPrompts.focus: comparing ideas and evaluating benefits for the future
speakingPrompts.prompt:
Discuss the following questions about museums and community activities. Give reasons for your opinions.
1. Why do some people visit museums often while others never visit them?
2. What are the advantages of free film-clubs and museum visits for a local community?
3. Will people still visit museums in the future when they can see everything online? Why or why not?
